subtitulo: The province of Achaea and the double condition of the Greek under Rome (146 BCE – 330 CE)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look for

items.text: First, the Arch of Hadrian and its two inscriptions, already described. The ten-minute detour is worth it; it is the most eloquent document of this installment and it stands out in the open, free, on a noisy avenue.

Second, the Odeon of Herodes Atticus. If there is a performance, go. A building financed in 161 CE by a provincial magnate for his own prestige, and which two thousand years later remains the most coveted venue in the country, is a lesson in the effectiveness of evergetism as a strategy for immortality. Compare it with the names on Lima's university foundations and auditoriums.

Third, in the National Archaeological Museum, the Roman portraits of the imperial era. Observe the change in gaze compared with classical sculpture: individuality, age, imperfection. And observe, too, how many of the "Greek" pieces we know are in fact Roman copies of lost originals. A good deal of what we call Greek art has come down to us because the Romans liked it enough to reproduce it in series. The canon of the West is, at its material base, a catalogue of reproductions commissioned by imperial collectors.

Fourth, in Corfu, if you have time left, the Roman remains at Palaiopolis and the baths beside the Mon Repos palace. Visually not much, but useful for confirming that the island spent four centuries as a naval waystation of an empire that used it without naming it.

coda.next_hint: The next installment makes the leap that is often skipped: how that Roman-Greek world becomes Christian and Eastern, why for a thousand years the Greeks called themselves ROMANS and not Hellenes, and how that self-designation — which survived in popular speech into the nineteenth century — was erased by nineteenth-century nationalism. It is the episode that explains why modern Greek identity is such a recent and such a contested artifact.

sections.heading: Horace's line and its trap
paragraphs: Around 10 BCE, Horace wrote the verse that sums up two millennia of misunderstanding: "Captive Greece took captive her fierce conqueror, and brought the arts into rustic Latium." The line is repeated as civilizational consolation — culture defeats arms — and functions, in fact, as one of the most precise formulations of colonial subordination that exist in ancient literature. Because what it describes is not a Greek victory: it describes the APPROPRIATION of a culture by a power that retains complete political and economic command. Greece did not conquer Rome. Rome consumed Greece, and granted it in exchange the prestige of having been consumed.

The proof lies in the simultaneity of two Roman attitudes that do not contradict each other but need each other. On one hand, the Roman elite educates its children in Greek, hires Greek tutors, collects Greek statues, philosophizes in Greek. On the other, Cicero — the most Hellenized of cultivated Romans — in his speech in defense of Flaccus, from 59 BCE, dismisses Greek testimony as frivolous and untruthful, and the diminutive GRAECULUS, "little Greek," circulates as a common insult designating the servile, glib, untrustworthy intellectual. Juvenal, a century and a half later, devotes an entire satire to expelling from Rome the hungry Greek who knows how to do everything and deserves no trust.

Hold onto this structure, because it is the thread of the whole installment and will reappear literally in 2010: the ancestor is venerated and the contemporary is despised, and both are part of the same apparatus. Venerating the ancestor allows one to claim the inheritance; despising the contemporary allows one to deny him the administration of that inheritance. The result is that the legitimate heir is excluded from his own patrimony on grounds of attributed incompetence. Any reading of Latin American indigenismo — the exaltation of the dead Inca alongside the contempt for the living Indian — recognizes the mechanism immediately. José María Arguedas devoted his work to dismantling it. Rome invented it first.

sections.heading: How Greece is subdued: 146, 86, 31 BCE
paragraphs: Subjugation was not a single operation but three staggered blows. The first, in 146 BCE, we have already seen: Mummius razes Corinth, sells its population, and ships its art to Italy. Polybius, a Greek historian, eyewitness and friend of the Scipios, writes the chronicle of the defeat of his own world from within the victors' camp. His great question — how Rome achieved in fifty-three years what no one had achieved before — inaugurates the analytical historiography of international relations, and his personal position, that of the peripheral intellectual who explains his own defeat in the language and for the audience of the victor, inaugurates something equally lasting.

The second blow is more revealing. In 88 BCE, Athens gambled on Mithridates VI of Pontus, who presented himself as the liberator of the Greeks from Roman fiscal extortion. It was the city's last autonomous foreign-policy decision, and it cost it everything: Sulla besieged Athens and took it in March of 86 BCE, sacking it with a violence the sources describe as blood running through the streets of the Kerameikos. Delos, the center of the Aegean slave trade, was devastated in 88 and again in 69 BCE, and never recovered. The message was clear: choosing wrong once is final. From then on, Greek politics consists of not choosing.

The third blow is indirect, and therefore more humiliating. For a century, Rome's civil wars were fought on Greek soil, with armies that Greece had to feed: Pharsalus in 48 BCE, Philippi in 42, and above all ACTIUM, on September 2, 31 BCE, at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, that is, less than a hundred kilometers south of Corfu, in waters you will see from the ferry or from the plane. There, between Octavian and Mark Antony, it was decided who would govern the Mediterranean world for the following four centuries; no Greek had a voice in the matter, and all paid for the logistics. Octavian founded on the site the city of Nicopolis and forcibly populated it with inhabitants from the cities of Acarnania and Aetolia, emptying them out. Being the stage for someone else's war, without being party to the conflict and paying its costs, is the operative definition of the strategic periphery. Greece will be this again in 1941, and Peru was this, in economic terms, during the War of the Pacific and the world wars that fixed the price of its exports without consulting it.

sections.heading: The province: depopulation, evergetism, and the Arch of Hadrian
paragraphs: The province of Achaea is organized in 27 BCE. What follows is a long period of peace and of demographic and economic decline. Plutarch, around 100 CE, writes that all of Greece could barely muster three thousand hoplites, the same number Megara alone had sent to Plataea six hundred years earlier. Strabo describes entire regions in ruins. The causes accumulate: wars, emigration, land concentration into great estates, the drain of surplus toward Italy, the shift of trade routes.

And yet Athens flourishes in a particular way: it becomes a university and a heritage destination. The children of the Roman elite — Cicero, Horace, and later the emperor himself — go to study philosophy and rhetoric in Attica. The city lives off its past. And around 150 CE, Pausanias writes the PERIEGESIS, ten books describing, monument by monument, what to see in Greece, what history each stone holds, and what cult is celebrated at each sanctuary. It is, literally, the first surviving travel guide in history, written for a public that already traveled to Greece to look at antiquities. Greek heritage tourism is nineteen hundred years old. When in September you walk through the Agora with a map, you will be repeating a second-century gesture.

The construction of those years depends on EVERGETISM: the private munificence of great patrons who fund public works in exchange for honors and statues. Herodes Atticus, the richest man in Greece in the second century, financed the odeon at the foot of the Acropolis still in use today — the Athens Festival programs performances there every summer, probably in September as well. And Hadrian, a philhellene emperor, rebuilt Athens, completed the Olympieion, which had stood unfinished for six hundred years, and founded in 131/132 CE the Panhellenion, a league of Greek cities whose admission criterion was demonstrating Hellenic ancestry before an imperial tribunal. Pause on that: GREEKNESS as a legal status granted by a Roman emperor of Spanish origin, upon prior documentary accreditation. Identity becomes a file administered from outside.

The monument that condenses all of this stands on Amalias Avenue, five minutes from Syntagma, and you can read it yourself. The Arch of Hadrian carries two inscriptions, one on each face. The one facing the old city reads: "This is Athens, the ancient city of Theseus." The one facing the new quarter reads: "This is the city of Hadrian, and not of Theseus." I know of no cleaner declaration in all of Antiquity of a substitution of authorship: the foreign benefactor carving in marble that the city now belongs to him. Think, standing before that arch, of the inauguration plaques on Peruvian public works, and whose name appears on them.

sections.heading: Roman citizenship: what Greece never learned to do
paragraphs: There is a technical difference between Rome and Greece that explains more than any consideration of national character. Athens closed its citizenship in 451 BCE to the children of an Athenian father and mother and kept it closed; it was a hereditary privilege whose value depended on its scarcity. Rome, by contrast, treated citizenship as an instrument of government: it granted it to allies, to freedmen, to entire communities, in degrees and by stages, until in 212 CE the Constitutio Antoniniana extended it to virtually all free inhabitants of the empire. The measure had evident fiscal motives — broadening the base of certain taxes — and that does not make it any less decisive.

The contrast matters because it defines two models of integration that are still operating today. One conceives belonging as an inheritance protected through restriction; the other, as a status granted in order to govern better. Neither is virtuous: universal Roman citizenship coexisted with mass slavery and with a growing legal inequality between honestiores and humiliores, which reintroduced through another door the hierarchy that citizenship had erased. That is: when formal status becomes universal, inequality migrates to the terrain of the differential application of the law. Anyone who has observed how equality before the law actually functions in Peru — where a proceeding stalls, to whom pretrial detention is applied, who has access to a defense — recognizes the phenomenon. Universal formal citizenship does not eliminate hierarchy; it makes it informal, and therefore harder to challenge.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: Han, Kushan, Moche
paragraphs: The first and second centuries CE are the moment of greatest connectivity in the ancient world. The Han empire in China and the Roman one in the Mediterranean, linked by the Silk Road through the Kushan and Parthian empires, move silk, spices, glass, and silver; Pliny complained of Rome's trade deficit with the East. Never before had so many people lived under so few states. And that integration had its price: the Antonine Plague of 165–180 CE, probably smallpox, arrived along the trade routes and killed perhaps ten percent of the population of the Roman empire. Ancient globalization spread pathogens with the same efficiency with which it spread goods, a lesson 2020 taught all over again.

In the Andes, this is the Moche period — roughly between the first and eighth centuries CE: coastal states with large-scale irrigation, metallurgy of the highest quality, monumental huacas of the Sun and the Moon, an elite of priest-warriors, and an explicit iconography of human sacrifice, confirmed archaeologically at the Huaca de la Luna. The Lady of Cao, discovered in 2006, further forced a revision of the assumption of exclusively male power. The pertinent parallel with Roman Greece is not one of content but of timescale: while the Mediterranean lives under a single imperial power, the Andes develop sophisticated, autonomous regional states, without unification. Universal history does not have a single clock, and the habit of dating everything by the Mediterranean calendar is itself a residue of the very operation this installment describes.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the cradle and the layabout
paragraphs: The structure of veneration and contempt that Cicero inaugurated reappeared with an almost obscene literalness during the Greek crisis. Between 2010 and 2015, the European press — the German press singularly, but not only — oscillated between invoking Greece as the cradle of democracy and of Europe, and describing contemporary Greeks as corrupt, tax-evading, and lazy, living beyond their means. The two images sustained each other: the glorious past made the unworthy present more scandalous, and that unworthiness justified tutelage. The OECD data on hours worked per year, in which Greece figured among the countries with the longest working hours in Europe, did not alter the narrative, because the narrative did not depend on the data.

The same device operates on Peru in the tourist and diplomatic register: international admiration for the Tahuantinsuyo, for Paracas textiles, for the cuisine, coexists without friction with the representation of the country as unstable, ungovernable, and incapable of administering its own patrimony. And the practical conclusion of that representation is always the same as in 1453, or in 1810, or in 2011 with the Yale pieces: legitimate custody must lie elsewhere. That is why patrimonial restitutions are not a sentimental matter. They are a dispute over who is recognized as capable of governing themselves.

There is an additional and more concrete resonance. Greece today sustains an economy in which tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of GDP, directly and indirectly, with more than thirty-five million visitors a year. That is: the country lives, in 2026 as in the second century, off others coming to look at what Greece once was. That dependency produces effects you will see on the ground: dual pricing, unaffordable housing in the historic centers of Athens and Corfu, precarious seasonal work, and a relationship with the visitor that mixes genuine hospitality — PHILOXENIA is a real and observable cultural norm — with an economic calculation no one bothers to conceal. The same tension exists in Cusco and in Ancash. Observe it without condescension: it is not hypocrisy, it is the normal effect of living off someone else's gaze.
